summary: The Remote Job Entry protocol, written by Bressler, Guida and McKenzie, for sending batch jobs to a remote server. A user controls the server over a Telnet connection to a special logger, and the server uses FTP to fetch the job input and deliver the output. It obsoletes RFC 360. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: You send a big job to another computer. It picks it up, does the work, and sends back the answers, like a laundry service for computing.

subtitle: How a user on the early ARPANET submitted a batch job to a remote host and got the output back.

tldr.problem: A user at one site wanted a batch-processing job run at some other site, with the input fetched from and the output delivered to places the user chooses.
tldr.mechanism: The user sends text commands over a TELNET connection to a special RJE logger at the server. The server then uses the File Transfer Protocol to retrieve the job-input file and to deliver the output files, and it answers every command with a numbered reply.
tldr.outcome: RFC 407 obsoletes RFC 360, and its status today is Historic.

facts.label: Control channel
facts.value: TELNET to the RJE Logger, socket 5

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 407 as Historic, and it obsoletes RFC 360. No RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: How Remote Job Entry Works
sections.content:
Remote job entry is the mechanism whereby a user at one location causes a batch-processing job to be run at some other location. The protocol specifies the standard procedures for a user to talk to a remote batch-processing server, causing it to retrieve a job-input file, process the job, and deliver the output file or files to a remote location.

All control traffic goes over a TELNET connection to a special standardized logger, the "RJE Logger" at socket 5, not socket 1. The server site then uses the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) to fetch the input and deliver the output. Users are either direct users (persons at a terminal) or user processes, and the commands and replies are designed to be readable by both.
sections.eli5: You talk to the other computer by typing messages to a special front desk. Behind the scenes, that computer fetches your work and later sends the answers where you asked.

sections.title: Commands and Output Handling
sections.content:
Each command is one line ending in the TELNET crlf. The first command on a new connection is USER, followed by PASS. Other commands set where the input comes from (INPUT, INPATH, INID, INPASS), where the output goes (OUT, OUTUSER, OUTPASS), and control a job or transfer (STATUS, CANCEL, ALTER, ABORT, REINIT, BYE, OP).

An output file can be sent then discarded, held only, or sent and saved. Commands such as CHANGE, RESTART, RECOVER, BACK, SKIP and HOLD reroute or steer output. Control cards starting with NET at the front of the input file can supply some of the same settings for a single job and take precedence over the TELNET commands.
sections.eli5: You type short orders like "start," "cancel" or "send my results over there." You can also write some orders on the first lines of the job itself.

sections.title: File Transfer Through FTP
sections.content:
Most files move through FTP. The RJE server calls its local User FTP, which connects to the FTP server in the other host. A new FTP connection is made for each file, with a data bytesize of 8 bits. Input uses Retrieve and output uses Append (with create). A <file-id> is either a host and socket for direct transfer, or a host and pathname handled through FTP.

The transmission option is T (TELNET-like coding), N (blocked records without carriage control) or A (blocked records with ASA carriage control), and the code is NVT ASCII or E for EBCDIC. On output, the server sends restart markers periodically (the RFC suggests about every 100 lines) so that RECOVER can restart a failed transfer. If the destination is busy or dead, the server should wait several minutes and try again.
sections.eli5: The computer uses a separate delivery truck, FTP, to pick up your job and drop off the answers. If the truck breaks down, it can pick up from a marker instead of starting over.

sections.title: Numbered Replies
sections.content:
Every server action, including each TELNET command, is answered with a reply made of a three-digit code, a blank and a text explanation. The code is for programs and the text is for people. The first digit gives the type of reply, the second digit the subject (for example x30 for primary log-on, x50 for FTP results, x60 for RJE results), and the last digit a particular message type.

Examples include 200 (last command received ok), 201 (an ABORT has terminated activity), 204 (a REINIT has been executed) and 230 (log-on completed). A reply that continues onto following lines starts with three blanks.
sections.eli5: After each order, the computer answers with a number and a sentence. The number is for machines, the sentence is for people.

items.label: Informative
items.desc: Issued voluntarily by the server to report some state of its system.

items.label: Status reply
items.desc: Answer to a specific status inquiry.

items.label: Positive acknowledgment
items.desc: Some previous command or request succeeded; 200 is a general ok.

items.label: Incomplete information
items.desc: No major problem, but activity cannot proceed with the input so far.

items.label: Unsuccessful
items.desc: A correct request could not be completed; further attempts need user commands.

items.label: Incorrect or illegal
items.desc: The command was invalid or inconsistent and was totally ignored.
